title: Constants & iota
summary: A **constant** is a value fixed at compile time — it can never change. Go constants can be *untyped*, which lets a numeric literal adapt to whatever type the context needs. `iota` is a compile-time counter that makes declaring sequences of related constants (like enums) clean and self-maintaining.

subtopics.title: Declaring constants
subtopics.explanation: `const` declares a value fixed at compile time. Constants can be characters, strings, booleans, or numbers — but only values the compiler can evaluate (no function results, no slices/maps). Because they are locked in before the program runs, they cost nothing at runtime and can never be reassigned. This is the foundation of the Constants & iota topic: every enum and bit-flag pattern begins with a `const` declaration.

subtopics.title: Untyped vs typed constants
subtopics.explanation: A constant without an explicit type is *untyped* and takes on a type from context, so `const N = 5` can be used as int, float64, etc. Adding a type (`const N int = 5`) fixes it to that type. Untyped constants also keep arbitrary precision until they are used somewhere concrete. Knowing this distinction matters throughout Constants & iota because untyped constants (including iota itself) flow into whatever numeric type each declaration needs.
subtopics.example:
package main

import "fmt"

const untyped = 5      // adapts to context
const typed int = 5    // locked to int

func main() {
	var f float64 = untyped // ok: untyped adapts
	var i int = untyped     // ok too
	fmt.Println(f, i, typed) // Output: 5 5 5
}

subtopics.title: iota: the constant counter
subtopics.explanation: Inside a const block, `iota` starts at 0 and increases by 1 with each line (each ConstSpec). It resets to 0 in every new const block. It's the idiomatic way to number a sequence of related constants without hand-writing the values. `iota` is the engine that powers the enum and bit-flag patterns at the heart of the Constants & iota topic.

subtopics.title: The enum pattern
subtopics.explanation: Define a named type plus a const block using iota to get type-safe enumerated values. Often the zero value is a meaningful 'unknown'/default, and adding a `String()` method gives readable output when printed. This is the canonical way Go expresses enums, combining named types with iota — a defining use case of the Constants & iota topic.

subtopics.title: Bit flags with iota
subtopics.explanation: Shift 1 by iota to make power-of-two flags you can combine with bitwise OR and test with AND. This packs multiple boolean options into one integer, just like Unix file permissions. Bit flags are one of the classic patterns the Constants & iota topic exists to teach, relying on iota's per-line increment to give each flag a unique bit.

subtopics.title: Skipping & expressions with iota
subtopics.explanation: You can skip values with the blank identifier `_` and apply an expression that repeats down the block with each new iota value. This powers patterns like KB/MB/GB scaling where every line multiplies the shift by 10. These advanced iota tricks round out the Constants & iota topic, showing how a single expression generates a whole family of related constants.

foundations.overview: Constants are values the compiler nails down before your program ever runs, so they can't change and cost nothing at runtime. Go adds a twist: many constants are *untyped*, meaning a literal like 42 doesn't commit to being an int until it's used in a context that needs a specific type. This makes constants flexible. The real star of this topic is `iota`, a tiny compile-time counter that increments once per line inside a const block. It turns the tedious, error-prone job of hand-numbering related constants (enums, bit flags, size multipliers) into a clean, self-maintaining declaration.
foundations.formalDefinition: A constant is a value of basic type (boolean, rune, integer, float, complex, or string) fixed at compile time. An untyped constant has a default type but adopts the type required by its context. iota is a predeclared identifier representing successive untyped integer constants, resetting to 0 at the start of each const block and incrementing by one per ConstSpec line.
foundations.whyItMatters: Constants make code safer (values can't be mutated) and faster (no runtime computation), and iota is the idiomatic Go way to build enums and flag sets. Understanding iota's per-line increment and how untyped constants adapt are common interview points and prevent subtle off-by-one enum bugs.
foundations.mentalModel: Picture a const block as a numbered list the compiler writes for you: iota is the line number, starting at 0. Each new line bumps the counter. Untyped constants are like flexible LEGO bricks that snap into whatever type-shaped hole you place them in.
commonUseCases: Bit flags combined with OR and tested with AND
Size multipliers (KB, MB, GB) via shifts
Named limits/timeouts instead of magic numbers

commonMisconceptions.reality: It resets to 0 at the start of every const block and increments per line within that block only.

commonMisconceptions.myth: All constants have a fixed type.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Untyped constants adopt a type from context; only constants declared with an explicit type are fixed.

commonMisconceptions.myth: iota increments per identifier in a line.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It increments once per ConstSpec line, regardless of how many names are on that line.

visualExplorer.caption: iota counts lines inside a single const block, starting at 0.

config.intro: Walking a const block to see what iota produces:

steps.name: Block starts, iota = 0
steps.detail: At the top of a const ( ... ) block, iota is 0. The first ConstSpec line uses that value.

steps.name: Each line increments iota
steps.detail: Every subsequent line increases iota by 1: line 0, 1, 2, ... regardless of names on the line.

steps.name: Expressions repeat
steps.detail: If a line has no expression, it reuses the previous line's expression with the new iota (e.g. 1 << iota gives 1,2,4,8).

steps.name: Skip with _
steps.detail: Using the blank identifier _ on a line consumes an iota value without naming a constant (handy to skip 0).

steps.name: New block resets
steps.detail: Start another const block and iota goes back to 0. It's scoped to the block, not global.

interactiveExamples.explanation: We declare a named type State and a const block where iota numbers the values 0,1,2. A String() method gives each value a readable name when printed.

interactiveExamples.title: Edit it: build combinable bit flags
interactiveExamples.explanation: Use 1 << iota to make power-of-two flags so they can be combined with | and tested with &. Fill in the const block so Read=1, Write=2, Exec=4, then combine and test them.

checkpoints.prompt: What values do A, B, C, D get?
checkpoints.code:
const (
	A = iota // ?
	B        // ?
	_        // skipped
	D        // ?
)
fmt.Println(A, B, D)
checkpoints.explanation: iota increments per line: A=0, B=1, the blank _ consumes 2, and D=3. The skipped line still advances iota, which is exactly why D is 3, not 2.
The expression repeats per line with the new iota. Line 0: 1<<(10*1)=1024. Line 1: 1<<(10*2)=1048576. That's the classic KB/MB pattern via shifting.

checkpoints.prompt: Why is an untyped constant like `const N = 5` useful?
options: It can be used where any compatible numeric type is needed (int, float64, etc.) without conversion
It runs faster than a typed constant
checkpoints.explanation: An untyped constant adopts the type required by its context, so N works as an int, a float64, etc., without an explicit conversion. Typed constants are fixed to one type.

checkpoints.prompt: This enum's values are all wrong (all 0). What's the bug?
checkpoints.code:
const Pending = iota
const Active = iota
const Closed = iota
options: Each separate const block resets iota to 0, so all are 0
checkpoints.explanation: iota resets to 0 at the start of every const block. Three separate const statements each restart it, so all values are 0. Put them in one const ( ... ) block to get 0,1,2.

codeLab.title: Implement a Level enum with names
codeLab.instructions: Define a Level type with constants Debug, Info, Warn, Error (in that order, starting at 0) using iota, and implement `func (l Level) String() string` returning the level's name. Then expose `Name(l Level) string` that returns it (for testing).
hints: Put all four constants in one const block so iota gives 0,1,2,3.
Type the first constant (Debug Level = iota); the rest inherit the expression and type.
Handle an out-of-range value with a default "UNKNOWN" in String().

debuggingLab.title: All enum values come out the same
debuggingLab.symptom: Printing the three statuses all shows 0, so comparisons like status == Active never behave as expected.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Each `const` on its own line is a separate const block, and iota resets to 0 in every block. So all three constants are 0 and become indistinguishable. iota only advances within a single const ( ... ) group.
commonMistakes: Writing each enum constant as its own const statement.
Assuming iota keeps counting across separate const declarations.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Group the constants in one const block so iota increments.

theory.question: What is iota and how does it work in a const block?
theory.directAnswer: iota is a predeclared, compile-time integer counter usable inside const blocks. It starts at 0 at the top of each const block and increments by 1 for every ConstSpec line, regardless of how many names are on that line. It resets to 0 in each new const block. It's the idiomatic way to declare numbered sequences like enums and bit flags.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A per-block, per-line auto-incrementing constant generator.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To declare related constants without hand-numbering them, so inserts/reorders renumber automatically.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The compiler substitutes iota with the line index within the block; expressions on a line repeat for following blank lines.

theory.whyImportant: Enums and flag sets are everywhere in Go; misunderstanding iota's reset/per-line rules causes subtle bugs.
theory.realWorldExample: Log levels (Debug, Info, Warn, Error) or HTTP-like state enums declared with iota.

followUps.question: What happens to iota on a blank (_) line?
followUps.answer: It still increments; the value is just discarded, which is how you skip 0 or reserve slots.

followUps.question: Does iota reset between const blocks?
followUps.answer: Yes — it resets to 0 at the start of every separate const block.

theory.question: What's the difference between a typed and an untyped constant?
theory.directAnswer: An untyped constant (const N = 5) has no fixed type and adopts the type required by its context, so it can act as an int, float64, etc., without explicit conversion, and it keeps high/arbitrary precision until used. A typed constant (const N int = 5) is locked to that type and behaves like a value of it. Untyped constants are more flexible; typed ones are more constrained.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two forms of constant differing in whether a type is fixed.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Untyped constants let literals work seamlessly across numeric types without conversions.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: An untyped constant takes its default type only when assigned/used somewhere that needs a concrete type.

theory.whyImportant: It explains why 1 << 40 works in float contexts and why some constant uses don't need conversions.
theory.realWorldExample: const Timeout = 30 used as both an int count and in a float64 calculation without conversion.

followUps.question: What's the default type of an untyped integer constant?
followUps.answer: int, when a concrete type is finally required and none is specified by context.

theory.question: How do you build a type-safe enum in Go using iota, and why add a String() method?
theory.directAnswer: Declare a named integer type and a const block that assigns iota to its values, e.g. type State int with Pending, Active, Closed. Using a distinct type (not plain int) makes the values type-safe so unrelated ints can't be passed where a State is expected. Adding a String() method on the type gives readable output when printed, since fmt calls it automatically via the Stringer interface.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The idiomatic Go enum: a named type plus iota-numbered constants and an optional String().
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Go has no enum keyword, so named types + iota provide type-safe enumerations.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: iota numbers the constants 0,1,2...; the named type enforces safety; String() satisfies fmt.Stringer for pretty printing.

theory.whyImportant: Enums are everywhere (states, levels, kinds); doing them idiomatically prevents mix-ups and unreadable logs.
theory.realWorldExample: Log levels Debug/Info/Warn/Error as a Level type with String() so they print as names, not numbers.

followUps.question: Why type the first constant (e.g. Pending State = iota)?
followUps.answer: The type and expression carry down the block, so the rest inherit State = iota without repeating it.

followUps.question: Is the zero value meaningful?
followUps.answer: Often yes — the first constant (iota 0) is commonly a sensible default like Pending or Unknown.

theory.question: How does an expression like 1 << iota repeat down a const block, and what does the blank identifier _ do there?
theory.directAnswer: If a const line has no explicit expression, it reuses the previous line's expression with the new iota value. So 1 << iota on the first line and blank lines below produce 1, 2, 4, 8 as iota goes 0,1,2,3. The blank identifier _ on a line consumes an iota value without naming a constant, which is how you skip 0 or reserve slots (e.g. _ = iota then KB = 1 << (10 * iota)).

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Expression repetition per ConstSpec line plus value-skipping with _.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To generate whole families of related constants from a single expression.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The compiler carries the last written expression to following blank lines, substituting the current iota; _ advances iota but binds no name.

theory.whyImportant: This powers bit flags (1 << iota) and size units (KB/MB/GB) — and misreading it causes off-by-one enum bugs.
theory.realWorldExample: const ( _ = iota; KB = 1 << (10 * iota); MB; GB ) yields 1024, 1MiB, 1GiB.

followUps.question: Does a _ line still advance iota?
followUps.answer: Yes — the value is just discarded, which is exactly why it's used to skip 0 or reserve positions.

scenario.question: You need a set of permission options that can be combined (read, write, execute) and stored compactly. How do you model them in Go?
scenario.directAnswer: Use bit flags declared with 1 << iota so each is a distinct power of two (Read=1, Write=2, Exec=4). Combine them with bitwise OR (Read|Write) into a single integer, and test membership with AND (perm&Write != 0). This packs several boolean options into one int and makes checks fast.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Bitmask flags built with iota and bit shifting.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To store and combine many on/off options efficiently in one value.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Each flag occupies a unique bit; OR sets bits, AND tests them, AND-NOT clears them.

scenario.whyImportant: Bit flags appear in file permissions, feature toggles, and protocol options.
scenario.realWorldExample: os.OpenFile flags (O_RDONLY, O_WRONLY, O_CREATE) are combined with OR.

followUps.question: How do you clear a flag?
followUps.answer: perm &^= Write (AND-NOT) clears the Write bit while leaving the others intact.

scenario.question: A teammate defined an enum as three separate const statements each set to iota, and every value comes out 0, breaking comparisons. What's wrong and how do you fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: iota resets to 0 at the start of every const block, and each separate const statement is its own block — so all three constants are 0 and become indistinguishable. Fix it by grouping them in a single const ( ... ) block so iota increments per line, giving 0, 1, 2.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A classic iota-reset bug from splitting an enum across multiple const blocks.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: iota is scoped to a single const block, not global, and restarts each block.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Within one const ( ... ) group iota increments per ConstSpec line; separate const statements each reset it to 0.

scenario.whyImportant: It silently breaks equality checks and switch statements on the enum, a subtle and common beginner trap.
scenario.realWorldExample: A Status enum whose Pending/Active/Closed all equal 0 makes status == Active always true (or never distinct).

followUps.question: Would gofmt or the compiler warn about this?
followUps.answer: No — it's valid code; all constants are legitimately 0, so you must catch it in review or tests.

systemDesign.question: You are designing a permissions model for a service where each resource grants some combination of read, write, and execute rights, stored compactly and checked fast. How would you model it in Go?
systemDesign.directAnswer: Model permissions as bit flags declared with 1 << iota so Read=1, Write=2, Exec=4, each occupying a unique bit. Store a resource's permissions as a single integer, combine rights with bitwise OR (Read|Write), test with AND (perm&Write != 0), and clear with AND-NOT (perm &^= Write). This packs multiple booleans into one word, is cheap to store and compare, and mirrors how Unix file permissions and os.OpenFile flags work.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A bitmask permission scheme built from iota and bit shifting.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To represent and combine many on/off options efficiently in one integer.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Each flag is a distinct power of two; OR sets bits, AND tests them, AND-NOT clears them.

systemDesign.whyImportant: Bitmask flags are compact and fast, and appear in file permissions, feature toggles, and protocol options.
systemDesign.realWorldExample: os.OpenFile combines O_RDONLY, O_WRONLY, and O_CREATE with bitwise OR — the same pattern.

followUps.question: How do you check a resource has ALL of several rights?
followUps.answer: Mask and compare: perm & (Read|Write) == (Read|Write) is true only if both bits are set.

followUps.question: What's the ceiling on number of flags?
followUps.answer: The bit width of the integer type — e.g. up to 64 flags in a uint64.

coding.question: Define KB, MB, GB constants using iota and shifting, and write func Human(n int64) string returning the largest fitting unit label (e.g. 2 for 2*MB -> "2MB").
coding.thoughtProcess: Use the _ = iota trick to skip 0, then 1 << (10*iota) doubles every 10 bits: KB=1024, MB=1<<20, GB=1<<30. Then divide n by the largest unit it exceeds.
coding.lineByLine: The first line consumes iota 0 with _ so KB starts at iota 1: 1<<(10*1)=1024. MB and GB reuse the expression with iota 2 and 3, giving 1<<20 and 1<<30. Human checks from largest to smallest unit and formats n divided by that unit; integer division is fine here since we want whole units.

followUps.question: Why skip the first iota with _?
followUps.answer: So KB lines up with iota 1 (1<<10); otherwise 1<<0 = 1 would be the first value.

followUps.question: How would you handle fractional units like 1.5GB?
followUps.answer: Use float64 division and a %.1f format instead of integer division.

coding.question: Define file-permission bit flags with 1 << iota and implement func Can(perm, want int) bool that reports whether perm includes ALL of the requested rights.
coding.thoughtProcess: Declare Read=1, Write=2, Exec=4 with 1 << iota so each is a distinct bit. To check that perm contains every requested right, mask perm with want and compare to want: perm & want == want.
coding.lineByLine: The const block uses 1 << iota so Read, Write, and Exec become 1, 2, 4 — each a unique bit. Can computes perm & want, which keeps only the requested bits that are actually set in perm; comparing that to want is true only when every requested bit is present. For example Can(Read|Write, Read) is true, but Can(Read, Read|Write) is false.

followUps.question: How would you test for ANY of the rights instead of all?
followUps.answer: Use perm & want != 0, which is true if at least one requested bit is set.

followUps.question: How do you add a right to perm?
followUps.answer: OR it in: perm |= Write sets the Write bit without disturbing the others.

keyTakeaways: Constants are values fixed at compile time with zero runtime cost; untyped constants adapt to the type their context requires.
iota is a compile-time counter that starts at 0 and increments once per line within a single const block, resetting in each new block.
Combine a named type + iota for type-safe enums (often with a String() method), and 1 << iota for combinable bit flags.
Watch the classic traps: separate const blocks reset iota, and blank (_) lines still advance it.
